findings.exposure_and_reference: Administrative district unit (시/군 여부): si (city) = 1 vs. gun (county) = 0 (Hypothesis 2), adjusted for mayoral reappointment, degree of financial independence, ln(local tax burden per person), private consignment, and local public enterprise status.
findings.finding_label: Administrative district tier (si vs. gun) on municipal Coulter inequity indices (H2)
findings.outcome_and_polarity: Municipality-level component of Coulter's coefficient of inequity (비형평성 계수) across 6 water indicators. Higher numerical values indicate GREATER inter-municipal distributional inequity (worse equity relative to population share Ei), NOT higher coverage or lower tariffs; furthermore, because Coulter compares Xi/sum(Xi) of non-additive rates/prices against population share Ei, lower Coulter inequity does not monotonically represent better household water access or lower household bills.

findings.exposure_and_reference: Degree of financial independence (재정자립도, continuous %): {(Local tax + non-tax revenue) / Total general accounting revenue} * 100 (2021 mean = 17.53%, SD = 11.16%, range 5.8%–58.5%; Hypothesis 3), adjusted for political, regional, tax-burden, and operational covariates.
findings.finding_label: Municipal degree of financial independence on Coulter inequity indices (H3)
findings.outcome_and_polarity: Municipality-level component of Coulter's coefficient of inequity across all 6 indicators. Higher numerical values indicate GREATER distributional inequity (worse equity in the author's framework, leading to rejection of H3); however, as noted in Footnote 14 (PDF pp. 8–9) and Table 7 (PDF p. 7), fiscally independent populous cities have high Coulter inequity scores even when they have ~98–100% piped coverage and LOWER household unit prices (405–629 won/m3), so this positive inequity coefficient does not mean worse household access.

findings.outcome_and_polarity: Municipality-level component of Coulter's coefficient of inequity across all 6 indicators. Higher numerical values mean GREATER distributional inequity; negative coefficients indicate LOWER Coulter inequity (higher inter-municipal equity in the author's framework, supporting H4), though the outcome is an indirect population-share proportionality deviation rather than household access or affordability.

headline_result_summary: In repeated cross-sectional analyses (2010, 2016, and 2021) of N = 152 South Korean basic local governments (si and gun), Ko (2024) first computes Coulter's population-share coefficient of distributional inequity across 6 municipal water indicators—average unit price, cost recovery rate, revenue water ratio, water supply rate, number of employees, and customer satisfaction (complaints)—finding that national inequity rose slightly between 2010 and 2021 for 5 of 6 indicators (most notably average unit price: 10.6 to 11.3; water supply rate: 9.5 to 10.4) and declined only for customer complaints (9.7 to 8.7). Second, cross-sectional Tobit regressions (Tables 9–14; confirmed via OLS in Appendix Table 15) regressing each municipality's Coulter inequity component (where HIGHER values mean GREATER inequity / WORSE equity) on political, administrative, fiscal, and operational factors yield mixed signs across predictors and null effects for utility-governance controls: (1) municipal financial independence (%) has a statistically significant positive coefficient across all 6 inequity indices in all 3 years (e.g., 2021 water supply rate inequity Coef. = .1382***, SE .0148; unit price inequity Coef. = .1353***, SE .0141), indicating GREATER inequity (rejecting H3); (2) city vs. county status (si = 1 vs. gun = 0) and natural-logged per-capita local tax burden have significant negative coefficients—indicating LOWER Coulter inequity—across 5 of 6 indices for si/gun (null for customer complaints; 2021 water supply rate inequity Coef. = -.8566***, SE .3149) and all 6 indices for per-capita local tax burden (2021 water supply rate inequity Coef. = -1.9333***, SE .5044); and (3) mayoral reappointment (H1), private consignment/outsourcing (Control I), and local public enterprise status (Control II) are statistically null across virtually all specifications (35 of 36 governance-control cells null; only 2010 private consignment on complaint inequity is +1.3224***, fading to null in 2016 and 2021). Crucially, in substantive household-access terms, the outcome in ALL regressions is an indirect population-share proportionality deviation (|Xi/S - Ei| scaled) rather than household water connection, service quality, or tariff affordability—and as Footnote 14 and Table 7 show, applying Coulter's formula to non-additive rates/unit prices mechanically scores populous, high-coverage, low-tariff cities as 'highly inequitable' and leads the author to prescribe urban tariff hikes.
specification_or_coding_pitfalls: Six major coding traps exist in this paper: (1) INVERTED DEPENDENT-VARIABLE POLARITY: Every regression in Tables 9–15 models Coulter's coefficient of INEQUITY (비형평성 계수), NOT water supply coverage, tariff level, or equity directly. Thus a POSITIVE (+) coefficient (as on Degree of financial independence) means GREATER inequity / WORSE equity, whereas a NEGATIVE (-) coefficient (as on Administrative district unit [si=1] and Local tax burden per person) means LOWER inequity / HIGHER equity. (2) COULTER NON-ADDITIVE RATIO ARTIFACT (CONFLATING COULTER INEQUITY WITH HOUSEHOLD ACCESS/AFFORDABILITY): In Coulter's formula, municipality i's share Xi/S of the 152-municipality sum S is compared against its population share Ei. When Xi is a non-additive percentage or unit rate (Water supply rate [%] or Average unit price [won/m3]), Xi/S is ~1/152 (0.66%) for every municipality while Ei is large in populous cities. Consequently, populous cities with high fiscal independence, ~98–100% piped coverage, and LOW household tariffs (e.g., 405–629 won/m3 in Table 7) are mechanically assigned high 'inequity' scores and prescribed massive tariff increases (e.g., +5,105 won/m3 for Gb 01 in Table 7; explicitly flagged as a limitation in Footnote 14, PDF pp. 8–9). This also explains why all five rate/count Tobit tables (Tables 9–13) produce nearly identical coefficients on Financial independence (~.10 to .16***), si/gun (~-.68 to -1.16), and Local tax burden (~-1.42 to -2.34***). Treating lower Coulter inequity as better household affordability or higher household coverage would invert substantive reality. (3) NULL GOVERNANCE / OWNERSHIP CONTROLS: If extracted for utility corporatization (`Local public enterprise status`) or private sector participation / delegated management (`Private consignment`), the effect is NULL across all water supply rate, unit price, cost recovery, revenue water, and staffing models in 2010, 2016, and 2021; a coder must not cherry-pick the single 2010 `Private consignment` cell in Table 14 (Customer complaints inequity = 1.3224***, while 2016 = .4449 and 2021 = .1356 are null). (4) TABLE MISLABELING IN ENGLISH: Table 1 (PDF p. 3) and Table 6 (PDF p. 7) misprint Coulter's 11–20 bracket ('minor inequity', Korean text p. 6: '약간 비형평한 수준') as 'minor equity'. (5) COPY-PASTE TYPOS BY AUTHOR: Table 12 (Water supply rate, PDF p. 11) and Table 13 (Number of employees, PDF p. 12) print identical LR chi2 (78.44, 55.98, 79.24), Pseudo R2 (0.1285, 0.0898, 0.1254), and Log likelihood (-265.9358, -283.7095, -276.4351) summary rows; on PDF p. 11, the Customer satisfaction paragraph erroneously repeats '상수도 보급률의 형평성' ('equity of water supply rate') when discussing operational controls; and Table 5 (PDF p. 6) prints Population SD as '250,34' instead of '250,343' stated in text. (6) BORDERLINE p<0.10 DIFFERENCES BETWEEN TOBIT AND OLS: `Administrative district unit` in 2010 Water supply rate is -.7195** (p<0.05) in Tobit Table 12 vs. -.720* (p<0.10) in OLS Table 15, and in 2016 Cost recovery rate (Table 10) and 2010 Revenue water ratio (Table 11) is significant only at p<0.10 (*).
study_design: Repeated cross-sectional observational study (2010, 2016, and 2021) at the municipal level using Coulter's coefficient of distributional inequity (Stage 1) and cross-sectional Tobit regressions with OLS multiple-regression robustness checks (Stage 2).
unit_and_sample_size: Basic local governments (si [cities] and gun [counties]) operating local water supply services in South Korea (excluding special/metropolitan cities and special self-governing provinces from 161 operators nationwide): N = 152 local governments analyzed separately in each of three cross-sectional years (2010, 2016, and 2021; Obs = 152 per model).
